Work through the examples in order. Section numbers follow the STA5001
lecture notes, which develop the models and algorithms used here. Open
`section-05.Rmd` in RStudio and choose **Knit** to reproduce the outputs.
Install BayesComp with `remotes::install_github("sj156/BayesComp", subdir = "BayesComp")`
to use the lecture-note figures included in this section.

# Section 5.2 — Evidence and prior sensitivity

**Concept.** A Bayes factor compares the probabilities or densities that two models
assign to the data after averaging over their parameters. Multiplying
prior odds by the Bayes factor gives posterior odds.

**Example.** After two heads, compare a fair coin with an alternative
that gives the head probability a uniform Beta prior. Then use the
lecture notes' standardized normal offset $z=2$ to see how increasing
the prior scale changes the evidence for a nonzero offset.

Subtract log marginal likelihoods to form the Bayes factor. For the
normal example, use marginal variance $1+s_0^2$ under the alternative
and compare its evidence with its conditional posterior mean.

```{r section5-evidence}
y_binary <- c(1, 1)
n_binary <- length(y_binary)
a0 <- b0 <- 1
log_m0 <- -n_binary * log(2)
log_m1 <- lbeta(a0 + sum(y_binary), b0 + n_binary - sum(y_binary)) -
  lbeta(a0, b0)
bf10 <- exp(log_m1 - log_m0)
prior_odds <- 1 / 3
posterior_m1 <- bf10 * prior_odds / (1 + bf10 * prior_odds)
stopifnot(abs(bf10 - 4/3) < 1e-12,
          abs(posterior_m1 - 4/13) < 1e-12)
c(Bayes_factor=bf10, posterior_alternative=posterior_m1)
s0 <- c(1, 10, 100)
z <- 2
normal_bf <- exp(-.5 * log1p(s0^2) + z^2 * s0^2 / (2 * (1+s0^2)))
data.frame(s0, posterior_mean=z*s0^2/(1+s0^2),
           Bayes_factor=normal_bf, model_probability=normal_bf/(1+normal_bf))
```

```{r s52-lecture-evidence, echo=FALSE, out.width="100%", fig.cap="Lecture notes, Section 5.2. The panels compare conditional estimation with model evidence."}
notes_figure("section52-evidence-sensitivity.png")
```

The two broad priors give almost the same conditional mean estimate, but
very different evidence. As an extension, change the observed value to
zero and explain the direction of every Bayes factor.

# Section 5.3 — Prior probabilities over model sizes

**Concept.** Model size aggregates prior probabilities over every subset of a
given size. The number of subsets therefore matters when translating
between priors on models and priors on model size.

**Example.** For two candidate predictors, compare fixed independent
inclusion with probability $1/2$ to a shared inclusion probability
drawn from a uniform Beta distribution.

Enumerate the four subsets, integrate each model probability using a
beta-function ratio, then sum the model probabilities by size.

```{r section5-prior-sizes}
gamma_small <- as.matrix(expand.grid(gamma1=0:1, gamma2=0:1))
size_small <- rowSums(gamma_small)
prior_fixed <- rep(1/4, 4)
a0 <- b0 <- 1
prior_mixed <- exp(lbeta(a0 + size_small, b0 + 2 - size_small) - lbeta(a0,b0))
stopifnot(abs(sum(prior_mixed)-1) < 1e-12)
data.frame(gamma_small, size=size_small, prior_fixed, prior_mixed)
sapply(0:2, function(s) sum(prior_mixed[size_small==s]))
```

For 20 predictors, compute the total probability of each size by
multiplying single-model probability by the number of models of that size.
The third prior puts more mass on smaller models.

```{r s53-twenty-predictors}
size <- 0:20
size_mass <- cbind(
  equal_models = dbinom(size, 20, .5),
  equal_sizes = rep(1 / 21, 21),
  sparse = exp(lchoose(20, size) + lbeta(1 + size, 40 - size) - lbeta(1, 20))
)
stopifnot(all(abs(colSums(size_mass) - 1) < 1e-12))
rbind(empty = size_mass[1, ], size_10 = size_mass[11, ],
      expected_size = drop(crossprod(size, size_mass)))
```

```{r s53-lecture-size, echo=FALSE, out.width="100%", fig.cap="Lecture notes, Section 5.3. The left panel shows aggregate size probabilities and the right shows per-model probabilities."}
notes_figure("section53-size-priors.png")
```

The mixed prior gives probabilities $(1/3,1/6,1/6,1/3)$ to the four
models. Try a beta prior with $(a_0,b_0)=(1,2)$ and compare its expected
size with the fixed-inclusion prior having the same mean inclusion rate.

# Section 5.4 — Exact enumeration and predictive uncertainty

**Concept.** When the model space is small enough to enumerate, normalize the
evidence-weighted prior probabilities directly. Model averaging then
uses those posterior weights to mix whole predictive distributions.

**Example.** Use the five artificial observations in the notes. The
two predictors are centered, and all variables are dimensionless.
The four models include every predictor subset and always an intercept.
Use $g_0=5$, equal model priors, and the shared nuisance prior
$p(\alpha,\sigma^2)\propto1/\sigma^2$ with the same constant in every
model. The computed evidences are ratios against the intercept-only model.

Compute the explained sum of squares for each subset, then transform its
fraction of the total into a Bayes factor. Normalize on the log scale,
sum weights for models that include each predictor, and average the
predictive variances at $(0,0)$, where the component means coincide.

```{r section5-enumeration}
dat5 <- data.frame(x1=c(-2,-1,0,1,2), x2=c(2,-1,-2,-1,2),
                   y=c(-1,0,1,1,4))
dat5
x5 <- as.matrix(dat5[c('x1','x2')])
yc5 <- dat5$y - mean(dat5$y)
n5 <- nrow(dat5)
g0 <- 5
gamma5 <- as.matrix(expand.grid(gamma1=0:1,gamma2=0:1))
size5 <- rowSums(gamma5)
r2_5 <- apply(gamma5, 1, function(included) {
  if (!any(included)) return(0)
  xs <- x5[, included==1, drop=FALSE]
  beta_hat <- solve(crossprod(xs),crossprod(xs,yc5))
  sum((xs %*% beta_hat)^2)/sum(yc5^2)
})
log_bf5 <- (n5-1-size5)/2*log1p(g0) -
  (n5-1)/2*log1p(g0*(1-r2_5))
normalize_log <- function(log_weights) {
  w <- exp(log_weights-max(log_weights))
  w/sum(w)
}
w5 <- normalize_log(log_bf5 + log(rep(.25,4)))
pip5 <- drop(crossprod(w5,gamma5))
q5 <- sum(yc5^2)*(1-g0*r2_5/(1+g0))
# At centered predictors (0,0), all predictive means are the sample mean.
# Integrating sigma^2 gives t_(n-1), with finite variance for n>3.
a_n5 <- (n5-1)/2
b_n5 <- q5/2
v5 <- (1+1/n5)*b_n5/(a_n5-1)
bma_variance5 <- sum(w5*v5)
data.frame(gamma5, R2=r2_5, BF=exp(log_bf5), posterior_weight=w5,
           predictive_variance=v5)
c(PIP1=pip5[1], PIP2=pip5[2], mean=mean(dat5$y), variance=bma_variance5)
# Independent checks: sum of probabilities, projection decomposition,
# normalization invariance, and direct marginal-likelihood integration.
stopifnot(abs(sum(w5)-1)<1e-12,
          abs(r2_5[4]-r2_5[2]-r2_5[3])<1e-12,
          max(abs(normalize_log(log_bf5-10000)-w5))<1e-10)
int5 <- vapply(seq_along(q5),function(j) {
  integrate(function(variance) (1+g0)^(-size5[j]/2) *
    variance^(-a_n5-1)*exp(-q5[j]/(2*variance)),
    0,Inf,rel.tol=1e-9)$value
},numeric(1))
stopifnot(max(abs(int5/int5[1]-exp(log_bf5)))<1e-7)
# Check the predictive variance against the t distribution's moments.
t_scale2 <- (1+1/n5)*q5/(n5-1)
stopifnot(max(abs(t_scale2*(n5-1)/(n5-3)-v5))<1e-12)
```

The full model explains more variation, but the first-predictor-only
model has higher posterior probability. At the centered prediction point,
model means agree while their predictive variances differ. The mixture
retains uncertainty even though the between-model mean term is zero.

Reweight the same likelihoods using an inclusion probability of 1/4.
Evaluate the four Student predictive densities on a common grid,
then plot the mixture for each model prior.

```{r section5-sensitivity}
omega <- .25
prior_sparse <- omega^size5*(1-omega)^(2-size5)
w_sparse <- normalize_log(log_bf5 + log(prior_sparse))
data.frame(gamma5, prior_sparse, posterior_weight=w_sparse)
c(PIP1=sum(w_sparse*gamma5[,1]), PIP2=sum(w_sparse*gamma5[,2]),
  predictive_variance=sum(w_sparse*v5))
y_future <- seq(-8,10,length.out=501)
dens5 <- sapply(seq_along(w5),function(j)
  dt((y_future-mean(dat5$y))/sqrt(t_scale2[j]),df=n5-1)/sqrt(t_scale2[j]))
plot(y_future,drop(dens5 %*% w5),type='l',lwd=2,col='#0072B2',
     xlab='Future response at centered predictors',ylab='Predictive density')
lines(y_future,drop(dens5 %*% w_sparse),lwd=2,lty=2,col='#D55E00')
legend('topright',c('Equal model priors','Inclusion probability 1/4'),
       col=c('#0072B2','#D55E00'),lty=c(1,2),lwd=2,bty='n')
```

As an extension, vary $g_0$ over $1,5,25$ and recompute both model
weights and within-model predictive variances. Changing only the weights
would miss the scale's effect on the conditional predictions.
